passage:
Wednesday, hostel room, 11 pm
Economics lecture today: slides in one tab, class chat in another, a shopping site in a third, plus my notes in a doc. I felt like a pilot with all the screens. Indu, sitting next to me, whispered, "Look at this boy, running an airport."
Tonight I opened my notes to revise. Half the sentences stop in the middle. One line just says "demand curve, ask later???" I can't remember a single example the professor gave, even though I was sitting right there. Payal's handwritten notes have three examples and a diagram.
I think every time I flicked to the chat, I lost the thread and caught up only halfway. It felt efficient. It wasn't.
Tomorrow: only the notes open, chat closed, phone in my bag. Let's see.
Harshad

qa.q: What does one line in Harshad's notes say?
qa.a: One line just says "demand curve, ask later???"

qa.q: Why did Harshad feel like a pilot during the lecture?
qa.a: Harshad felt confident and in control with slides, chat, a shopping site and notes all open, so the rapid switching seemed efficient rather than costly.

qa.q: What choice does Harshad make for tomorrow, and how can he tell if it works?
qa.a: Only the notes open, chat closed, phone in the bag; comparing tomorrow's notes with today's broken sentences will show whether it helps.

qa.q: What do Payal's handwritten notes suggest about how the lecture went for Payal?
qa.a: With three examples and a diagram, Payal seems to have followed the professor steadily, which shows the lecture could be followed with full attention.

grounding: It shows a male student with many tabs open during a lecture who feels efficient but ends up with broken notes and little memory.

passage:
After the statistics lecture, Siddhant messages his classmates Minakshi and Bhavna.
Siddhant: can someone send today's notes 🙏
Minakshi: weren't you in the front row?
Siddhant: yes, laptop open the whole time. recording, group chat and the fest planning sheet. totally on top of it
Bhavna: so what was the second test she explained?
Siddhant: ...the one with the table?
Bhavna: there were three tables 😅
Minakshi: you were typing in the fest sheet during the example. we could see
Siddhant: I was listening though. I thought I was
Siddhant: ok honestly I remember the fest sheet better than the lecture
Minakshi: sit with us on Thursday. laptop closed, one notebook. fest stuff after class
Siddhant: deal. and please still send the notes

qa.q: What three things did Siddhant have open on the laptop?
qa.a: Siddhant had the recording, the group chat and the fest planning sheet open.

qa.q: Why did Siddhant believe he was "totally on top of it"?
qa.a: Having everything open and switching quickly felt like handling it all; only when Bhavna asked about the second test did he find the lecture hadn't stuck.

qa.q: What plan does Minakshi suggest for Thursday, and why could it work?
qa.a: Sitting together with the laptop closed and one notebook, and doing fest work after class, removes the switching so the lecture gets full attention.

qa.q: How do Minakshi and Bhavna see Siddhant's lecture habits?
qa.a: They noticed the typing in the fest sheet during the example, so they aren't surprised by the request for notes; they tease a little and then offer a practical fix.

grounding: It shows a male student who thinks he can follow a lecture, a chat and a planning sheet at once, but remembers little of the lecture.

passage:
At the district college, Chetan was the only one in his row with a laptop, a gift from his uncle. During the botany lecture he kept his notes file open, and beside it a cricket score page and a chat with his friends from the bus. He felt sharp, switching every minute.
Leela, sitting behind him with a thin spiral notebook, wrote steadily.
That evening, on the crowded bus home, they revised for Friday's test. Leela read out the parts of the flower from her notebook. Chetan scrolled through his file: fragments, a missing diagram, "sepal?? petal??"
"You were typing the whole hour," Leela said.
"Typing the wrong things," Chetan admitted. The next day he kept the score page closed and sat beside her.

qa.q: What did Leela read out on the bus?
qa.a: Leela read out the parts of the flower from her notebook.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel sharp while switching every minute?
qa.a: Chetan felt clever and confident, because moving quickly between the notes, the score and the chat felt active, so he assumed he was catching everything.

qa.q: What did Chetan change the next day, and why might it help?
qa.a: He kept the score page closed and sat beside Leela, cutting the switches so the lecture could get his attention.

qa.q: How might Leela see the difference between her notebook and Chetan's laptop?
qa.a: Leela may see that the plain notebook kept her with the lecture, while the laptop's extra pages pulled Chetan away despite being the fancier tool.

grounding: It shows a male student in a small-town college who switches between notes, scores and chat, feeling sharp while his notes suffer.

passage: In a lecture hall at a university in Istanbul, Emre sat with his laptop open to four things at once: the economics slides, his notes file, a chat with his football team, and a page of cheap flights home to Izmir. Elif, beside him, wrote in a paper notebook. "I'm following everything," Emre whispered. "Notes, slides, chat. Efficient." When the professor asked him what price elasticity meant, he said, "Um, it was on the slide?" That evening Leila from the study group asked him to share his notes. Emre opened the file: half-sentences, a line that just said "demand something", and a flight price. Elif's notebook had three clear examples and a diagram. Emre scrolled through his own notes twice, as if the rest might appear.

qa.q: What four things did Emre have open on his laptop?
qa.a: The economics slides, his notes file, a chat with his football team, and a page of cheap flights home to Izmir.

qa.q: Why did Emre believe he was following everything?
qa.a: Having everything open at once felt efficient and busy, so he didn't notice how little of the lecture was actually going in.

qa.q: What could Emre try in the next lecture?
qa.a: He could close the chat and the flights page, keep only his notes open, and check messages after class, so the lecture gets his full attention.

qa.q: How might Leila feel reading Emre's notes?
qa.a: Leila probably felt disappointed and a bit amused, having asked for help and got half-sentences and a flight price 😅

grounding: A student with slides, notes, chat and other tabs open believes he is following the lecture, but his notes and memory show otherwise.

passage: In the computer lab at the engineering college in Warangal, Ganga ma'am was explaining loops on the big screen. Farhan had three windows open: the code editor, the class chat and a live cricket score. He typed along with her, replied to a joke in the chat, checked the score, came back. "I'm keeping up with everything," he told the boy next to him. At the end, Ganga ma'am set a ten-minute exercise: write a loop to print a times table. Farhan stared at his editor. His code had half of her example and three typos. He couldn't remember why the loop stopped. The boy next to him, who had only the editor open, was already done. Farhan closed the cricket window, then the chat, and started again from the first line.

qa.q: What exercise did Ganga ma'am set at the end?
qa.a: Write a loop to print a times table.

qa.q: What does Farhan closing the cricket window and the chat suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he realised the switching had cost him, and felt frustrated enough to try again with his full attention.

qa.q: What turning point does the exercise give Farhan, and what could he do from now on?
qa.a: Being stuck while his neighbour finished showed the cost of switching; he could keep only the editor open in lectures and check chat and scores afterwards.

qa.q: How might Ganga ma'am see Farhan during the lecture?
qa.a: She may have seen a student typing busily and assumed he was keeping up, without knowing how much of her example he was missing.

grounding: A student switching between code, chat and a cricket score feels he is keeping up, until he cannot write the loop he just watched.
